claims.claim: Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome Atlas on 2026-09-08: a ~1-petabyte precomputed dataset covering all ~9 billion possible single-nucleotide variants in the human genome, described as more than 30 times larger than the AlphaFold Database.

The AVI (AlphaGenome Variant Impact) score is trained on proxy labels derived from the gnomAD v4.1 population-group-max filtering allele frequency at a 0.1% threshold — that is, on rarity, not on curated pathogenicity — using 18 input features.
AVI is published on a PHRED-like percentile rank scale running 0 to approximately 80, where 10 means the top 10% most impactful variants genome-wide, 20 the top 1%, and 30 the top 0.1%.
On ClinVar intronic SNVs the Atlas paper reports AVI AUPRC 0.76 versus 0.44 for the next-best model GPN-Star-V; on synonymous 0.57 versus CADD v1.7's 0.35; on 3'UTR 0.50 versus GPN-Star-M's 0.18.

AVI is beaten on ClinVar 5'UTR SNVs by GPN-Star-V (0.27 versus 0.26) and on TraitGym Mendelian variants by GPN-Star-M (0.77 versus 0.76); the paper's error bars are 95% confidence intervals from 100 bootstraps, so both 0.01 margins are non-differences.
On a splicing exon-extension task the specialist predictors are effectively tied with AVI: AVI/AlphaGenome 0.943, SpliceAI 0.940, Pangolin 0.939, against GPN-Star-V 0.348 and CADD v1.7 0.289.

In DeepMind's retrospective rare-disease benchmark on 112 known likely-pathogenic variants, AVI ranked the causal variant in the top 50 candidates 29.5% of the time versus 12.5% for CADD v1.7; after applying a gnomAD allele-frequency filter of 0.001 the figures rise to 74.3% and 61.0%.
gnomAD v4 reports 786,500,648 SNVs passing quality control from 807,162 individuals — under a tenth of the roughly 9 billion arithmetically possible single-nucleotide substitutions in GRCh38.

CADD has precomputed deleteriousness scores for all possible human SNVs since 2014 and is free only for non-commercial use, so the count of 9 billion scored variants is not itself novel; the Atlas's differentiator is depth, at roughly 27,000 experiment-specific predictions per variant.

ClinGen's SVI calibration of PP3/BP4 sets local positive likelihood-ratio thresholds of 2.406 (Supporting), 5.790 (Moderate), 33.53 (Strong) and 1,124 (Very Strong) against an estimated 4.41% prior probability of pathogenicity.

ClinGen's calibration found CADD's developer-recommended threshold of 20.0 falls in the score interval corresponding to moderate evidence for BP4 (benign), with a local LR+ of 0.157, and that CADD at that default flags 65.1% of gnomAD variants as damaging against a 4.41% prior.
ClinGen SVI calibration found AlphaMissense's developer-recommended cutoff of 0.564 does not reach even the Supporting level of evidence; the recalibrated PP3_Strong threshold is 0.990.

Sasse et al. found Enformer achieved Pearson R = 0.58 across 13,397 genes but a mean cross-individual R of 0.01 across 839 ROSMAP individuals, with 195 of 598 significantly predicted genes (33%) anti-correlated with observed expression.

In the same study a PrediXcan elastic-net baseline significantly predicted 921 genes to Enformer's 162 on the 1,570 shared genes (mean R 0.26 versus 0.02) and never predicted the wrong direction of effect.

Huang et al. reported across-gene Spearman correlations of 0.57 (Enformer), 0.52 (Basenji2), 0.53 (ExPecto) and 0.33 (Xpresso) on Geuvadis data (n=421, 3,259 eQTL genes), while the distribution of cross-individual correlations was centered close to zero for all four models.

Karollus et al. found Enformer correlated r = 0.81 with measured promoter strength but only r = 0.137 with enhancer strength in the same assay, and underestimated validated enhancer effects roughly fivefold (median predicted ~4% versus ~20% measured).

GTEx v8, the source of AlphaGenome's expression and splicing supervision across 49 tissues, comprises 838 donors of whom 715 (85.3%) are European American, 103 (12.3%) African American and 12 (1.4%) Asian American.

The Human Pangenome Reference Consortium's 47-assembly draft adds 119 million base pairs of euchromatic polymorphic sequence and 1,115 gene duplications relative to GRCh38 — sequence that has no coordinate in an atlas enumerated on GRCh38.
UK Biobank participants are 94.6% of white ethnicity, and the Atlas's flagship population-genetics case study ran on over 54,000 UK Biobank participants without any stated ancestry stratification.

The Zoonomia project estimates at least 332 million bases — about 10.7% of the human genome — are unusually conserved across 240 mammals, far below ENCODE's contested 80.4% biochemical-activity figure, so covering the non-coding 98% of coordinates is not the same as covering functional sequence.
ClinVar held 4,561,224 variation records as of 2026-09-08, of which 2,373,336 (52.0%) carry an uncertain-significance classification against 423,738 (9.3%) pathogenic or likely pathogenic.

In the largest published reclassification cohort only 7.7% of unique variants of uncertain significance were ever reclassified, and 91.2% of those were downgraded to benign or likely benign rather than upgraded.

Manrai et al. found 5 of 94 variants previously reported as causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were too common in the general population to be pathogenic, and seven patients — all of African or unspecified ancestry — had already received positive reports.

Kurian et al. reported adjusted bilateral-mastectomy probabilities among average-pretest-risk breast-cancer patients of 85% with a pathogenic mutation, 51% with only a variant of uncertain significance, and 42% with no mutation detected; among lower-volume surgeons, 50% managed BRCA1/2 VUS the same as pathogenic mutations.

In a single-laboratory cohort of 36,684 people with no personal cancer history tested on one 30-gene panel, the HBOC and Lynch VUS rate was 5.8% for European-ancestry patients, 12.3% for African-ancestry patients and 13.1% for Asian and Pacific Islander patients, while pathogenic detection ran the other way at 7.6% versus 2.4% and 4.3%.
In 493,515 Invitae probands, African American or Black patients had a VUS rate of 46% against 32% for non-Hispanic white patients, and a pathogenic germline variant rate of 9% against 13%.

FDA's Clinical Decision Support Software guidance, reissued 2026-01-29, explicitly lists a prioritized list of options as an acceptable non-device output, but requires that the software let a clinician independently review the basis of the recommendation, including a description of the data relied upon and of validation results and their limitations.

ClinGen retired its Sequence Variant Interpretation Working Group in April 2025 and marked its general recommendations, including the PP3/BP4 calibration, as archived in July 2025, directing users to a newer variant classification guidance page.

The AlphaGenome Atlas prospective analysis ranked de novo variants in 814 individuals with parent-and-proband genomes from the GREGoR Consortium, and the only new diagnosis publicized is a single DNM1 variant.

A dedicated deep-intronic and non-canonical splicing sweep across 38,688 individuals in the 100,000 Genomes Project produced 35 candidate new diagnoses of which only 6 were confirmed molecular diagnoses.

MaveDB, the central repository for multiplexed assays of variant effect, held over 7 million variant effect measurements across 1,884 datasets as of November 2024 — under 0.1% of the 9 billion variants the Atlas scores, and dominated by protein rather than regulatory assays.

The AVI static score table is licensed for commercial and non-commercial use, while the AlphaGenome Atlas feature attributions that explain the score are non-commercial only, and the API terms forbid using outputs to train other machine learning models.

Carl de Boer of the University of British Columbia, who is unaffiliated with DeepMind, said of the Atlas's single-number impact score that it has a clear use but is probably going to be easily misinterpreted.
Google DeepMind states that AlphaGenome has not been validated for, and is not approved for, any clinical use, and describes the Atlas as a baseline rather than an endpoint.

The published AlphaGenome Nature paper claims the model matches or exceeds the strongest available external models in 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations; in the preprint the figure was 24 of 26, and the named loss is MFASS, where Pangolin scored auPRC 0.54 against AlphaGenome's 0.51.

An independent evaluation of AlphaGenome on personal genomes found it clearly beat Enformer but still lagged plain Elastic Net and Random Forest models trained on individual-level data, with about 28% of its predictions still anti-correlated with observed expression.
CADD's own documentation tells users to rank candidates for follow-up rather than hard-filter on a cutoff, and states that there is not a natural choice of threshold because it is always arbitrary.

The 100,000 Genomes Project pilot achieved genetic diagnoses in 25% of probands, of which 14% came via the combined research and automated pathway that non-coding, structural and mitochondrial findings travel through.

The comparator set in the Atlas's genome-wide benchmarks consists of CADD v1.7 and GPN-Star; REVEL, BayesDel, VEST4, MutPred2, Enformer, Borzoi, Evo 2 and ESM do not appear as baselines, while GPN-Star's own paper benchmarks against a strictly larger set.

AlphaFold2 won CASP14 with a summed z-score of 244.02 against the runner-up's 90.82 in a blinded prospective third-party assessment; no equivalent blinded assessment of AlphaGenome or the AVI score exists, because CAGI7's prediction season closed in December 2025.
